## Assignment week 4: what went well

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**Time structure modeling**

- Most submissions correctly followed the "time structure first" approach
- Polynomial terms (quadratic and/or cubic) were appropriately tested using likelihood ratio tests
- Random slope testing was generally done correctly with `refit = FALSE`
- ICC calculations and interpretations were accurate

**Adding covariates**

- Good use of `step()` for backward elimination of fixed effects
- Most correctly identified significant Gender × time interactions
- Interpretation of interaction effects was generally clear and meaningful

**Diagnostics and interpretation**

- Residuals vs. fitted plots were included in most submissions
- Interpretation of the diagnostic plots generally correct but be wary of overinterpretation: minor deviations in the loess curve at the extremes are normal, especially where data is sparse

:::

## [Residual diagnostics: linear vs quadratic vs cubic]{style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Load the growth data
asian_data <- read.csv("../labs_2526/data/asian_data.csv")
asian_data <- asian_data |>
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
asian_data$age_c <- asian_data$Age - mean(asian_data$Age)

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(gridExtra)
library(emmeans)

# Fit three models
model_linear <- lmer(Weight ~ age_c + (age_c | ChildID),
                     data = asian_data,
                     control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

model_quad <- lmer(Weight ~ poly(age_c, 2, raw = TRUE) + (age_c | ChildID),
                   data = asian_data,
                   control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

model_cubic <- lmer(Weight ~ poly(age_c, 3, raw = TRUE) + (age_c | ChildID),
                    data = asian_data,
                    control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

# Create diagnostic data frames
diag_linear <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(model_linear), residuals = resid(model_linear))
diag_quad <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(model_quad), residuals = resid(model_quad))
diag_cubic <- data.frame(fitted = fitted(model_cubic), residuals = resid(model_cubic))

# Create plots
p1 <- ggplot(diag_linear, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Linear model", x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p2 <- ggplot(diag_quad, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Quadratic model", x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p3 <- ggplot(diag_cubic, aes(x = fitted, y = residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = TRUE, color = "blue", fill = "lightblue", linewidth = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Cubic model", x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3)
```

- **Linear model**: Clear curvature in the loess line — time trend not adequately captured
- **Quadratic & cubic models**: Loess line close to zero throughout — both are adequate fits
- Minor deviations at the extremes (where data is sparse) are **not** evidence of model misfit

## Assignment week 4: areas for improvement

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**Time trend specification**

- A few submissions used only linear time despite the quadratic term being significant
  - Always carry forward the time structure you established when adding covariates
- When adding Gender, include interactions with **all** polynomial terms you retained

**The marginality principle**

- Some students correctly questioned whether polynomial terms should be treated as a unit
- Good practice: if you include Age³, you should generally keep Age² and Age even if not individually significant
- This also applies to testing interactions: test Gender × time as a block, not term-by-term

**Plotting mean trajectories**

- Several submissions produced jagged "mean trajectory" plots (see next slide)
- This happens when using `geom_line()` on means computed at each unique (unrounded) age
- **Solution**: Use `geom_smooth()` or round ages to whole months before computing means

:::

## Plotting mean trajectories: a common mistake

::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Problematic approach**

```r
# Computing means at each exact age
mean_traj <- data |>
  group_by(Age) |>
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(Weight))

# Produces jagged line!
geom_line(data = mean_traj, 
          aes(Age, mean_wt))
```

- Ages are measured precisely (6.2, 6.3, 6.5 months...)
- Often only 1-2 observations per exact age value
- "Mean" at each point is very noisy

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

**Better approaches**

```r
# Option 1: Use geom_smooth()
geom_smooth(aes(x = Age, y = Weight), 
            method = "loess", se = FALSE)

# Option 2: Round ages first
mean_traj <- data |>
  mutate(Age_rounded = round(Age)) |>
  group_by(Age_rounded) |>
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(Weight))

# Option 3: Use stat_summary()
stat_summary(aes(x = Age, y = Weight),
             fun = mean, geom = "line")
```

- Smoothing or binning produces interpretable trajectories
- Always consider: do my time points align across individuals?

:::

:::

## Mean trajectories: incorrect vs correct

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5

# Incorrect: means at each exact age with geom_line
mean_traj_exact <- asian_data |>
  group_by(Age) |>
  summarise(mean_wt = mean(Weight, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

p_incorrect <- ggplot(asian_data, aes(x = Age, y = Weight)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = ChildID), alpha = 0.1, color = "grey60") +
  geom_line(data = mean_traj_exact, aes(x = Age, y = mean_wt),
            color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = mean_traj_exact, aes(x = Age, y = mean_wt),
             color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Incorrect: geom_line() on exact age means",
       subtitle = "Jagged line due to few observations per exact age",
       x = "Age (months)", y = "Weight (grams)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Correct: using geom_smooth
p_correct <- ggplot(asian_data, aes(x = Age, y = Weight)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = ChildID), alpha = 0.1, color = "grey60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Correct: geom_smooth() with loess",
       subtitle = "Smooth trajectory captures the underlying trend",
       x = "Age (months)", y = "Weight (grams)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

grid.arrange(p_incorrect, p_correct, ncol = 2)
```

## Using `poly()` for polynomial terms

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**Manual polynomial terms** (what most of you used)

```r
data$age_c2 <- data$age_c^2
data$age_c3 <- data$age_c^3
model <- lmer(Weight ~ age_c + age_c2 + age_c3 + (age_c | ChildID), data = data)
```

**Using `poly()` instead** (cleaner approach)

```r
model <- lmer(Weight ~ poly(age_c, 3, raw = TRUE) + (age_c | ChildID), data = data)
```

**Advantages of `poly()`**

1. **Cleaner code**: No need to create separate squared/cubic variables
2. **Correct `step()` behavior**: Tests Gender × poly() interaction as a block, respecting marginality
3. **Easier `emmeans`**: Works seamlessly without duplicated factor level errors

**Note**: Use `raw = TRUE` for interpretable coefficients. Without it, `poly()` creates orthogonal polynomials (useful for reducing collinearity but coefficients are harder to interpret).

:::

## Using `emmeans` to interpret interactions

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

**Why use `emmeans`?**

- Raw coefficients in models with interactions are conditional effects (e.g., effect of Gender when Age = 0)
- These conditional effects are often not meaningful or interpretable
- `emmeans` (estimated marginal means) lets you probe the interaction at meaningful values

**Example: probing a Gender × Age interaction**

```r
library(emmeans)

# Estimated marginal means at specific ages
emmeans(model, ~ Gender | Age, at = list(Age = c(6, 12, 18, 24)))

# Pairwise comparisons at each age
emmeans(model, pairwise ~ Gender | Age, at = list(Age = c(6, 12, 18, 24)))
```

**Interpretation approach**

1. First establish that the interaction is significant (use `anova()` or `step()`)
2. Then use `emmeans` to understand **where** and **how much** the effect differs
3. Report the estimated means and/or pairwise differences at clinically relevant time points

:::

## [Linear regression as a conditional distribution model]{style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 6

library(gridExtra)
library(grid)

# Simulate simple linear regression data
set.seed(42)
n <- 200
x <- runif(n, 0, 10)
y <- 2 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(n, 0, 2)
sim_data <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

# Two specific x values for histograms
x_low <- 2
x_high <- 8

# Get observations near these x values
tol <- 0.8
data_low <- sim_data[abs(sim_data$x - x_low) < tol, ]
data_high <- sim_data[abs(sim_data$x - x_high) < tol, ]

# Expected means
mu_low <- 2 + 1.5 * x_low
mu_high <- 2 + 1.5 * x_high

# Main scatter plot with regression line
p_main <- ggplot(sim_data, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "gray50") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_low, linetype = "dashed", color = "#E69F00", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = x_high, linetype = "dashed", color = "#56B4E9", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = data_low, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#E69F00", size = 2) +
  geom_point(data = data_high, aes(x = x, y = y), color = "#56B4E9", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "X", y = "Y", title = "Linear regression: Y = β₀ + β₁X + ε") +
  annotate("text", x = x_low, y = max(y) - 1, label = paste0("X = ", x_low), color = "#E69F00", fontface = "bold", hjust = -0.1) +
  annotate("text", x = x_high, y = max(y) - 1, label = paste0("X = ", x_high), color = "#56B4E9", fontface = "bold", hjust = -0.1) +
  theme_minimal() +

# Histogram for X = 2
p_hist_low <- ggplot(data_low, aes(x = y)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#E69F00", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_low, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  xlim(range(y)) +
  labs(x = "Y", y = "Count", title = paste0("Distribution of Y | X = ", x_low)) +
  annotate("text", x = mu_low + 0.5, y = Inf, label = paste0("μ = ", mu_low), vjust = 2, hjust = 0, fontface = "italic") +
  theme_minimal() +

# Histogram for X = 8

  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#56B4E9", color = "white", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_high, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", linewidth = 1) +
  xlim(range(y)) +
  labs(x = "Y", y = "Count", title = paste0("Distribution of Y | X = ", x_high)) +

# Arrange plots

```

## Linear regression in GLM notation

Linear regression is really a model for **conditional distributions**: it assumes that $Y|X$ follows a normal distribution with mean determined by the regression line:

$$Y_i | X_i \sim N(\mu_i, \sigma^2) \quad \text{where} \quad \mu_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$$

- The regression line gives the **conditional mean**: $E[Y_i | X_i] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$
- At each value of $X$, observations are **normally distributed** around this mean
- The variance $\sigma^2$ is constant across all values of $X$

::: {style="margin-top: 0.8em;"}
**This is a Generalized Linear Model (GLM):**

- A GLM specifies a **distribution** for $Y|X$
- The **mean** of this distribution is modeled as a function of predictors

Linear regression is a GLM with a normal distribution. We can generalize to other distributions for different outcome types.
:::

## Logistic regression as a GLM

:::{style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

**You already know logistic regression for binary outcomes** (e.g., disease yes/no)

**Distribution:** Individual outcomes follow a Bernoulli distribution:
$$Y_i | X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)$$

**Mean:** The expected value is the probability of success: $E[Y_i] = \pi_i$

**The problem:** We want to model $\pi_i$ as a linear function of predictors, but:

- The linear predictor $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$ can be any real number
- The probability $\pi_i$ must be between 0 and 1

**The solution: a link function:**
$$\text{logit}(\pi_i) = \log\left(\frac{\pi_i}{1 - \pi_i}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i$$

The logit link transforms probabilities (0, 1) to the real line ($-\infty$, $+\infty$)

:::

## Generalized linear models: the framework

**Three components define a GLM:**

1. **Random component:** Distribution of $Y_i | X_i$ from the **exponential family** (normal, binomial, Poisson, ...)

2. **Systematic component:** Linear predictor $\eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{pi}$

3. **Link function:** $g(\mu_i) = \eta_i$ connects the mean $\mu_i = E[Y_i | X_i]$ to the linear predictor

**Common GLMs:**

:::{style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

| Model | Distribution | Link | $g(\mu)$ | Constraint solved |
|:------|:-------------|:-----|:---------|:------------------|
| Linear regression | Normal | Identity | $\mu$ | None needed |
| Logistic regression | Bernoulli/Binomial | Logit | $\log(\frac{\mu}{1-\mu})$ | $\mu \in (0,1)$ |
| Poisson regression | Poisson | Log | $\log(\mu)$ | $\mu > 0$ |

:::

## The Poisson distribution

**The Poisson distribution models count data** (e.g., number of events in a fixed period)

**Its probability mass function:**

$$P(Y = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!} \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$$

where $\lambda$ is the average number of events (rate parameter)

**Key properties:**

- $E[Y] = \lambda$
- $\text{Var}[Y] = \lambda$ (mean equals variance!)
- Assumes counts are independent and occur at a constant rate

## Visualizing the Poisson distribution

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Create data for different lambda values
lambda_values <- c(1, 3, 5, 10)
x_range <- 0:20

poisson_data <- expand.grid(x = x_range, lambda = lambda_values) |>
  mutate(probability = dpois(x, lambda),
         lambda_label = paste0("λ = ", lambda))

ggplot(poisson_data, aes(x = x, y = probability, fill = factor(lambda))) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Rate parameter") +
  labs(
    title = "Poisson Distribution for Different Values of λ",
    x = "Number of events (k)",
    y = "Probability P(Y = k)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

As $\lambda$ increases, the distribution shifts right and becomes more symmetric.

## Poisson regression as a GLM

**Poisson regression models count outcomes as a function of covariates:**

$$Y_i | X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda_i)$$

**The mean $\lambda_i$ must be positive**, so we use the **log link**:

$$\log(\lambda_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{pi}$$

Or equivalently:

$$\lambda_i = \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_p X_{pi})$$

**Key assumption:** Mean equals variance ($E[Y] = \text{Var}[Y] = \lambda$)

## Case study: Heart failure hospitalizations

**Research questions:**

- How does age influence the number of hospitalizations for heart failure?
- What is the impact of comorbidities on hospitalization rates?

**Data description:**

- Simulated dataset of 1,000 individuals
- Variables:
  - Age (in years)
  - Comorbidity status (binary: yes/no)
  - Number of hospitalizations for heart failure (count outcome)

```{r}
# Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(123)

# Simulate data
n <- 1000
heart_failure_data <- data.frame(
  age = round(rnorm(n, mean = 65, sd = 10)),
  comorbidity = rbinom(n, 1, 0.4)
)

# True model: log(lambda) = -2.1 + 0.033*age + 0.375*comorbidity
heart_failure_data$lambda <- exp(-2.1 + 0.033 * heart_failure_data$age +
                                   0.375 * heart_failure_data$comorbidity)
heart_failure_data$hospitalizations <- rpois(n, heart_failure_data$lambda)

# Center age for interpretation
heart_failure_data$age_c <- heart_failure_data$age - mean(heart_failure_data$age)

# Convert comorbidity to factor with effect coding
heart_failure_data$comorbidity_f <- factor(heart_failure_data$comorbidity,
                                            levels = c(0, 1),
                                            labels = c("No", "Yes"))
contrasts(heart_failure_data$comorbidity_f) <- contr.sum(2)

# Create age groups for visualization
heart_failure_data$Age_Group <- cut(heart_failure_data$age,
                                     breaks = c(-Inf, 60, 70, Inf),
                                     labels = c("<60", "60-70", ">70"))
```

```{r}
gridExtra::grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3)
```

## Fitting the Poisson regression model

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

```{r}
# Fit Poisson regression model (age centered, comorbidity with effect coding)
poisson_model <- glm(hospitalizations ~ age_c + comorbidity_f,
                     family = poisson(link = "log"),
                     data = heart_failure_data)

summary(poisson_model)
```

:::

## Interpreting Poisson regression coefficients

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Extract coefficients
coefs <- coef(poisson_model)
b0 <- coefs["(Intercept)"]
b1 <- coefs["age_c"]
b2 <- coefs["comorbidity_f1"]

rate_intercept <- exp(b0)
rr_age <- exp(b1)
```

**Fitted Poisson regression model:**

$$\log(\lambda) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}_c + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Comorbidity}$$

**The log link means coefficients represent multiplicative effects on rates:**

- **Intercept ($\beta_0$ = `r round(b0, 3)`):** The log of the baseline rate
  - Back-transform to get rate: $\exp(\beta_0)$ = `r round(rate_intercept, 2)` hospitalizations per year

- **Age ($\beta_1$ = `r round(b1, 3)`):** For each 1-year increase in age, the log rate increases by `r round(b1, 3)`
  - **Rate ratio**: $\exp(\beta_1)$ = `r round(rr_age, 3)` — each additional year multiplies the rate by `r round(rr_age, 3)`

- **Comorbidity:** Comparing groups requires estimating group-specific rates → Use `emmeans`!

## Using `emmeans` for rate ratios

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Estimated rates for each comorbidity group (back-transformed)
emmeans(poisson_model, ~ comorbidity_f, type = "response")
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
# Rate ratio comparing comorbidity groups
pairs(emmeans(poisson_model, ~ comorbidity_f), type = "response")
```

**Note:** The infinite df reflects that GLMs use asymptotic (large-sample) inference based on the normal distribution, rather than the t-distribution.

:::

## Model diagnostics

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

**Pearson residuals:** measure the standardized difference between observed and expected counts:

$$r_i = \frac{Y_i - \hat{\lambda}_i}{\sqrt{\hat{\lambda}_i}}$$

where $Y_i$ is the observed count and $\hat{\lambda}_i$ is the expected count (mean)

**Chi-square goodness-of-fit test:**

- Test statistic: $\chi^2 = \sum r_i^2 = \sum \frac{(Y_i - \hat{\lambda}_i)^2}{\hat{\lambda}_i}$
- Degrees of freedom: $n - p$ (observations minus parameters)
- Interpretation: $p > 0.05 \Rightarrow$ Model fits the data well

**Dispersion parameter:** $\hat{\phi} = \chi^2 / (n - p)$

- $\hat{\phi} \approx 1$: Poisson assumption (mean = variance) holds
- $\hat{\phi} > 1$: Overdispersion (variance > mean)
- $\hat{\phi} < 1$: Underdispersion (rare)

:::

## Model diagnostics for our model

```{r}
#| echo: false

# Calculate Pearson residuals and fitted values
heart_failure_data$Pearson_Residuals <- residuals(poisson_model, type = "pearson")
heart_failure_data$fitted <- fitted(poisson_model)

# Chi-square test statistic
chisq_test <- sum(heart_failure_data$Pearson_Residuals^2)
df <- nrow(heart_failure_data) - length(coef(poisson_model))
p_value <- 1 - pchisq(chisq_test, df)
dispersion <- chisq_test / df
```

| Diagnostic | Value |
|:-----------|------:|
| Chi-square statistic | `r round(chisq_test, 2)` |
| Degrees of freedom | `r df` |
| p-value | `r round(p_value, 4)` |
| **Dispersion parameter** | **`r round(dispersion, 2)`** |

**Interpretation:**

- p-value > 0.05: no evidence of lack of fit
- $\hat{\phi} \approx 1$: mean = variance assumption holds

## Dealing with overdispersion

**Overdispersion** ($\hat{\phi} > 1$) means variance exceeds the mean, violating the Poisson assumption.

**Consequences if ignored:**

- Standard errors are **underestimated**
- p-values are too small → inflated Type I error
- Confidence intervals are too narrow

**Quasi-Poisson model:**

- Assumes $\text{Var}(Y) = \phi \cdot \mu$ instead of $\text{Var}(Y) = \mu$
- Estimates $\phi$ from the data (the dispersion parameter we calculated)
- **Adjusts standard errors** by multiplying by $\sqrt{\hat{\phi}}$
- Coefficient estimates remain unchanged; only inference is corrected


# Lab 7 – Poisson Regression

## [Poisson regression with aggregated count data]{style="font-size: 0.90em;"}

**So far:** Poisson regression on individual-level data

- One row per person
- Outcome: number of asthma exacerbations per individual
- Predictors: age, smoking status

**Now:** Poisson regression on aggregated count data

- One row per group (defined by covariate combinations)
- Outcome: total events within each group
- Challenge: groups have different amounts of **exposure time**

**Key concept:** The **offset** term accounts for varying exposure

## Why work with aggregated count data?

**Practical reasons:**

- **Cohort studies**: Data naturally collected as event counts per person-years of follow-up
- **Administrative data**: Hospital infection counts per patient-days
- **Privacy**: Individual data not available, only group-level summaries

**Statistical validity:**

- For count data, aggregation preserves sufficient statistics
- Poisson regression on aggregated data gives identical results to individual-level analysis (when all relevant covariates define the groups)

## Case study: Cardiovascular disease events

**Research questions:**

- How does age affect the rate of cardiovascular events?
- How is smoking status associated with the rate of events?

**Data description:**

- Aggregated cohort data with groups defined by age and smoking status
- Variables:
  - Outcome: Number of cardiovascular events (count)
  - Exposure: Total person-years of follow-up per group
  - Predictors:
    - Age group: Young (18–40), Middle-aged (40–60), Older (60–75), Elderly (>75)
    - Smoking status: Non-smokers, light smokers (<10 pack-years), moderate smokers (10-20 pack-years), heavy smokers (>20 pack-years)

```{r}
# Create aggregated cardiovascular data
set.seed(456)

cardio_data <- expand.grid(
  Age_Group = factor(c("18-40", "40-60", "60-75", ">75"),
                     levels = c("18-40", "40-60", "60-75", ">75")),
  Smoking_Status = factor(c("Non-smoker", "Light smoker", "Moderate smoker", "Heavy smoker"),
                          levels = c("Heavy smoker", "Moderate smoker", "Light smoker", "Non-smoker"))
)

# Simulate person-years and events
cardio_data$Person_Years <- round(runif(16, 500, 2000))

# True rates based on age and smoking
base_rate <- 0.03
age_effects <- c(1, 3.2, 4.7, 9.5)  # Relative to youngest
smoking_effects <- c(1, 0.67, 0.57, 0.57)  # Heavy smoker as reference

cardio_data$rate <- base_rate *
  age_effects[as.numeric(cardio_data$Age_Group)] *
  smoking_effects[as.numeric(cardio_data$Smoking_Status)]

cardio_data$Events <- rpois(16, cardio_data$rate * cardio_data$Person_Years)
```

## Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 5

library(gridExtra)

cardio_data$Event_Rate <- cardio_data$Events / cardio_data$Person_Years * 1000

# Plot 1: Event rates
p1 <- ggplot(cardio_data, aes(x = Age_Group, y = Event_Rate, 
                        color = Smoking_Status, group = Smoking_Status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Smoking Status") +
  labs(
    title = "Event Rates",
    x = "Age Group",
    y = "Rate (per 1000 person-years)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

# Plot 2: Person-years (exposure)
p2 <- ggplot(cardio_data, aes(x = Age_Group, y = Person_Years, 
                        color = Smoking_Status, group = Smoking_Status)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Smoking Status") +
  labs(
    title = "Exposure Time",
    x = "Age Group",
    y = "Person-Years of Follow-up"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

grid.arrange(p1, p2, ncol = 2)
```

**Key observations:** 

- Event rates increase with age and differ by smoking status
- Groups have **different amounts of exposure time** (person-years)
- We need to account for this variation in our model

## The challenge: varying exposure time

::: {style="font-size: 0.90em;"}

**Our data structure:**

- 16 groups (4 age categories × 4 smoking levels)
- Each group has:
  - **Events**: Count of cardiovascular events
  - **Person_Years**: Total follow-up time (exposure)
  - **Rate**: Events / Person_Years

**The problem:**

- We want to model **counts** (Events), not rates
- But groups with more person-years naturally have more events
- Simply modeling counts would bias toward high-exposure groups

**The solution: offset term**

- $\log(\text{Expected Events}) = \log(\text{Person Years}) + \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Smoking}$
- The $\log(\text{Person Years})$ term has a fixed coefficient of 1

:::

## Statistical model specification

::: {style="font-size: 0.90em;"}

**What we're actually modeling:**

$$\text{Events}_j \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu_j)$$

where the expected count $\mu_j$ depends on exposure and covariates:

$$\mu_j = \text{Person_Years}_j \times \lambda_j$$

**Taking logs:**

$$\log(\mu_j) = \log(\text{Person_Years}_j) + \log(\lambda_j)$$

**The Poisson regression equation:**

$$\log(\lambda_j) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age Group}_j + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Smoking Status}_j$$

**Putting it together:**

$$\log(\mu_j) = \underbrace{\log(\text{Person_Years}_j)}_{\text{offset}} + \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}_j + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Smoking}_j$$

:::

## [Fitting the Poisson regression model with offset]{style="font-size: 0.90em;"}

```{r}
#| echo: true

# Fit Poisson model with offset and interaction
poisson_cardio <- glm(Events ~ Age_Group + Smoking_Status + offset(log(Person_Years)),
                      family = poisson(link = "log"),
                      data = cardio_data)

# Type III ANOVA using car package
car::Anova(poisson_cardio, type = "III", test.statistic = "LR")
```

## Aggregated Poisson vs multi-level models

**The key question: Do you have individual-level data?**

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Aggregated Poisson**

- Data: One row per **group**
- Example: 16 rows (4 age groups × 4 smoking levels)
- Can only use group-level predictors
- No individual variation modeled

**When to use:**

- Only group summaries available
- All relevant predictors are categorical
- Research focus on group comparisons
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Multi-level models**

- Data: One row per **individual**
- Example: 5,000 rows (patients in hospitals)
- Can use both individual and group predictors
- Models within-group variation with random effects

**When to use:**

- Individual data available
- Want to adjust for individual characteristics
- Natural clusters (hospitals, schools)
:::

::::

## Example: Hospital infection rates

**Research question:** How do staffing levels affect infection rates?

:::: {.columns style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Aggregated approach:**

```r
# Data: 20 rows (one per hospital)
hospital_data
# Hospital  Infections  Patient_Days  Staffing
# 1         45          2500          0.8
# 2         32          2100          1.2
# ...

glm(Infections ~ Staffing + 
    offset(log(Patient_Days)),
    family = poisson)
```

**What you can answer:**

- Do hospitals with better staffing have lower infection rates?

**What you cannot answer:**

- Does patient age affect infection risk?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Multi-level approach:**

```r
# Data: 50,000 rows (one per patient)
patient_data
# PatientID  Hospital  Infected  Age  Staffing
# 1          1         0         45   0.8
# 2          1         1         72   0.8
# ...

glmer(Infected ~ Age + Staffing + 
      (1|Hospital),
      family = binomial)
```

**What you can answer:**

- How does patient age affect infection risk?
- Do hospitals with better staffing have lower rates?
- How much variation exists between hospitals?
:::

::::

## [Generalized Linear Mixed Effects Models (GLMMs)]{style="font-size: 0.9em;"}

**GLMMs extend GLMs to account for grouped or clustered data**

- Incorporate random effects to model within-group correlations

**Example: binary outcome (hospital infection status)**

- Outcome: Infection status ($Y_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}$) for patient $i$ in hospital $j$
- Fixed effects: Age, comorbidities (individual-level) and staffing ratios (context-level)
- Random effects: Hospital-specific effects ($u_j$)

**Model specification:**

$$\text{logit}(\pi_{ij}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot \text{Age}_{ij} + \beta_2 \cdot \text{Staffing}_j + u_j$$

$$u_j \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2)$$
